From the numbers alone, intense public antipathy for Donald Trump's economic
record makes no sense. Our economy has not crashed.

Unemployment, which [measured](https://www.reuters.com/business/us-job-growth-
slows-sharply-september-unemployment-rate-rises-42-2026-10-02/) 4.2% in
September, remains well below the 21st century average. Inflation, 3.4% year-
over-year [in August](https://www.reuters.com/markets/us/us-inflation-rises-
less-than-expected-august-consumer-spending-surges-2026-09-30/), exceeds the
25-year average by less than one percentage point. Overall growth, currently
projected at 2.3% this year by the Federal Reserve, tracks the economy's long-
term potential.

That scoreboard cannot explain why only 26% of Americans
[approved](https://apnews.com/article/trump-economy-approval-trump-
midterms-8d5809758a31b29c73f4351a8008147c) of Trump's economic performance in
an Associated Press/NORC poll last week - a number that has Republicans
fearing a midterm elections catastrophe.

What can explain it: Two years after campaigning on a promise of rapid
improvements, Americans see that his policies have made things worse. And if
that weren't bad enough, the billionaire president openly
[scorns](https://www.npr.org/2025/12/11/nx-s1-5639957/trump-affordability-
hoax-economy-midterms) their struggles with affordability as "a hoax."
